body.html:
Some teachers buy points-tracking apps. This summer, I built my students a private adventure guild — and it turned a five-day bilingual camp into the loudest classroom in the building.

Our whole camp ran on an ongoing TRPG saga — Legend of the Little Oyster: The Green Chopstick Uprising (《小蚵人傳說：綠竹筷的逆襲》) — in which the arrogant Golden Spoon Chef locks away every legendary recipe in Tainan, and teams of little heroes train, cook, and speak English to win them back. And this time, that entire quest ran on a classroom system I built myself: 【Little Oyster Adventure Guild (小蚵人冒險公會)】.

Here's what's inside it, how it was built, and how it survived five days in a real classroom.

Why Build Instead of Buy?

Ready-made classroom apps are great — until your class needs something they were never designed to do.

I wanted my students' daily effort to become visible growth: today a higher level, tomorrow cooler gear, and the whole class teaming up against a bigger boss. That kind of world can't be configured. It has to be built.

So I built it. The planning started the week the July camp wrapped up, and I kept building right up until the August one opened — weeks of nights, weekends, and a growing stack of AI subscriptions. Every line of it written by me, with AI as my coding partner.

From Zero to Guild in Minutes

The question every teacher asks first: "How long does setup take?"

Minutes. Here's the whole onboarding:

(And before anyone asks — building it took me over a month of evenings. Setting it up takes minutes. Those are two very different things.)

No student accounts. No passwords to reset. Scan, join, play.

Inside the Guild

A quick tour of what the kids actually see and do:

🎎 Paper-doll avatars — skin tone, expression, hat, weapon. Every kid gets to be their own little oyster.

⚔️ Quests & EXP — solve English missions, earn experience, level up, unlock titles. Effort finally has a shape.

👗 Rare drops — complete a quest and gear might drop… including the low-probability "apron" set that became the most talked-about treasure of the whole camp.

🐉 Guild boss raids — the entire class whittles down one big boss together. Nobody is a bystander.

🎲 The Fate Altar — dice multipliers turn every single award into drama.

🛒 Market price-guessing — kids guess prices on their tablets; my screen reacts instantly and hands out EXP automatically. Same moment, two screens:

🖥️ One classroom screen — clock, countdown, announcements, videos, draggable widgets. My co-teachers' absolute favorite: they couldn't stop saying how useful it was.

The Teacher's Cockpit

The part nobody sees from the student side — and the reason my co-teachers kept saying it made their days easier:

The Honest Truth About "Building It With AI"

If you think AI-assisted development means dictating a wish list and watching code appear — no.

It is nights of back-and-forth: change a line, test once, change it again. It is describing a classroom problem precisely enough that the machine understands what a teacher actually needs. And yes, that meant still editing the system at 12:30 a.m. the night before the camp opened.

There were real costs, too — and I'd rather say it before someone assumes otherwise: monthly AI subscriptions that quietly piled up, an entire summer of building from dawn till dark, and a friend with IT experience who set up the server for me because server administration was beyond what I could learn in time.

AI made a solo teacher-developer possible. It did not make it effortless — or cheap.

The Field Had Other Plans

Then reality joined the project.

Day 1: my server died — the computer running it belonged to a friend, he was abroad, and his family couldn't get back to restart it until 4 p.m. So I ran the day on a buggy older build, fixed the real server myself that first camp night, and merged the records back the next morning.

Day 1 (lunchtime): a family of three bats moved onto our classroom ceiling. We relocated. The kids were... enthusiastic.

Day 2: our classroom's domain got blocked (dynamic DNS, apparently). I sent one email to the office in charge — and to my surprise, they had it whitelisted in about half an hour.

What amazed me: the kids never noticed the system had been swapped mid-camp. For them, the adventure simply continued.

The Online Banquet

One shared goal above them all: the online banquet.

…racing to combine ingredients into legendary dishes worth bonus EXP. They debated recipes like seasoned chefs — and cheered like a stadium crowd.

What the Kids Taught Me

1. A shared boss unites a class more than individual points ever will.

2. Scarcity is magic — the rare apron made them line up for quests for five straight days.

3. Tools exist for the teaching, not the other way around. Save the teacher one minute of fumbling, give it back to the kids.

A classroom is already a world. Sometimes it just needs its own game. 🎮

If you're building education technology, researching teacher-made tools, or you're an educator who'd love something like this for your own classroom — let's connect. I'm happy to share how it was built, what it really cost, and what I'd do differently.

And if you simply want to swap stories about turning learning into an adventure — that works too.

body.html_zh:
有些老師買現成的記分軟體。今年夏天，我為學生打造了一座專屬的冒險者公會——把為期五天的雙語營隊，變成了整棟大樓最熱鬧的教室。

我們整個營隊都運行在一場持續推進的 TRPG 傳奇戰役中——《小蚵人傳說：綠竹筷的逆襲》（Legend of the Little Oyster: The Green Chopstick Uprising）。故事中，傲慢自負的金湯匙總鋪師鎖住了台南所有的傳奇食譜，而小勇士小隊必須經過訓練、動手烹飪並開口說英語，才能奪回這些名菜。而這一次，這場完整的冒險全都在我自己親手打造的課堂系統上運行：【小蚵人冒險公會（Little Oyster Adventure Guild）】。

以下是這座公會的內部面貌、它的開發歷程，以及它如何在真實課堂的五天實戰中挺過考驗。

為什麼要自己做，而不直接買現成的？

現成的教學軟體很棒——直到你的課堂需要一些它們從未設計過的功能。

我希望學生的每日付出能化為看得見的成長：今天升了一級、明天拿到更酷的裝備，全班還能一起組隊挑戰更強大的 Boss。那樣的世界無法靠現成設定拼湊出來，它必須被親手打造。

於是我著手動工。規劃始於七月營隊結束的那一週，我一路寫程式直到八月營隊正式開營——熬過無數個夜晚與週末，AI 訂閱費也悄悄堆得越來越高。每一行程式碼都由我親手寫下，以 AI 作為我的程式夥伴。

幾分鐘內，從零直達公會

每位老師首先會問的問題都是：「設定要花多久時間？」

幾分鐘。以下是完整的引導入門流程：

（在大家問之前先說明——打造這個系統花了我一個多月的所有夜晚；但設定它只需要幾分鐘。這兩者截然不同。）

學生不需要註冊帳號，不需要重設密碼。掃碼、加入、直接開玩。

公會內部巡禮

快速帶大家看看孩子們實際上看到與操作的內容：

🎎 紙娃娃虛擬造型——膚色、表情、帽子、武器自由搭配。每個孩子都能化身專屬的小蚵人。

⚔️ 任務與經驗值（EXP）——破解英語任務、賺取經驗、提升等級、解鎖稱號。努力終於有了具體的形狀。

👗 稀有掉落物——完成任務就有機會掉落裝備……包括那套低機率的「圍裙」套裝，它成了整個營隊討論度最高的頂級寶物。

🐉 公會 Boss 團戰——全班合力削弱一隻大 Boss 的血量。沒有任何人是旁觀者。

🎲 命運祭壇——骰子倍率讓每一次獎勵都充滿戲劇張力。

🛒 菜市場猜價遊戲——孩子們在平板上猜價格，我的螢幕即時連動並自動發放經驗值。同一時刻，雙螢幕同步互動：

🖥️ 一體化課堂大螢幕——時鐘、倒數計時、公告、影片、可拖曳小工具。這是協同教師們的最愛：他們一直誇讚這功能到底有多好用。

教師指揮艙

學生端看不見的後台核心——也是我的協同夥伴們不斷說這套系統讓他們教學變得輕鬆許多的秘密：

關於「用 AI 開發」的誠實告白

如果你以為 AI 輔助開發就是念出許願清單然後看著程式碼憑空出現——並不是。

那是無數個反覆拉鋸的夜晚：改一行 code、測試一次、再改一次。那是必須極其精準地描述課堂教學問題，機器才能理解身為第一線老師到底需要什麼。是的，這意味著在營隊開幕前夕的半夜 12 點半，我依然在修改系統。

而且背後有真實的成本——我寧可先坦白說清楚，以免有人過度理想化：默默累積的每月 AI 訂閱費、整個夏天從天明寫到天黑的漫長工時，還有一位懂 IT 的朋友幫我架設伺服器，因為伺服器維運遠遠超出我短時間內能學會的範圍。

AI 讓「單槍匹馬的教師兼開發者」成為可能。但它從未讓這件事變得輕而易舉——也絕不便宜。

真實教學現場總有別的劇本

接著，現實直接撞進了這個專案。

第 1 天：我的伺服器當機了——運行主機屬於那位朋友，而他當時人在國外，家人直到下午 4 點才能趕回家重開機。於是我用帶有一堆小 bug 的舊版本撐過第一天，在營隊第一個晚上自己動手修復正式伺服器，隔天一早將所有紀錄無縫合併回去。

第 1 天（午餐時間）：一家三口的蝙蝠直接搬進了我們教室的天花板。我們只能緊急換教室。孩子們則是……無比興奮。

第 2 天：我們教室的網域被教育局阻擋了（據說是動態 DNS 的緣故）。我寄了一封信給負責單位——令我驚喜的是，他們大約半小時內就把它列入了白名單。

最讓我驚嘆的是：孩子們根本沒察覺系統在營隊中途被偷偷調換過。對他們來說，冒險只是自然而然地繼續進行。

線上辦桌盛宴

高懸在所有小隊之上的共同終極目標：線上辦桌。

……大家爭分奪秒合成傳奇菜餚以換取額外經驗值。他們像老練大廚一樣激烈爭論食譜——並像球場觀眾席一樣瘋狂歡呼。

孩子們教會我的三件事

1. 共同的 Boss 比個人積分更能凝聚全班。

2. 稀缺性就是魔力——那套稀有圍裙讓孩子們連續五天排隊接任務。

3. 工具是為教學服務，而不是本末倒置。幫老師省下一分鐘手忙腳亂，就能多還給孩子一分鐘。

一間教室本身就是一個世界。有時候，它只是需要屬於自己的遊戲。🎮

如果你正在投入教育科技開發、研究教師自製工具，或者你也是一位希望能為自己課堂帶來類似體驗的教育工作者——歡迎與我交流。我很樂意分享這套系統是如何打造的、背後真正的成本，以及如果重來一次我會做哪些不同的調整。

如果你只是想聊聊把學習變成一場冒險的故事——也非常歡迎。

body.html:
🏕️ Five days. One bilingual camp. A family of bats, a buggy backup server, and a birthday song from a classroom of kids.

I just finished my second bilingual summer camp in Tainan. Everyone keeps asking how it went, so here is the honest version.

The Worst Opening Ever

The night before, I had a fever and was still editing my classroom gamification app at 12:30 a.m. I set my alarm for 5:30, actually woke up at 6:55, and sprinted to camp looking like I had been hit by a truck — apologizing all the way to my classmate who was already waiting downstairs.

Then the server died. That morning. It lived on a friend's computer. He was abroad. The fix would arrive at 4 p.m. So we ran the day on a buggy older build — just enough to record experience points, plus a “please save the save-file” pact — and I fixed the real server that night. The records merged back seamlessly the next day.

Then Came the Bats

At noon, a student pulled the curtain and found... black things. One bat. Then two. A family of three, roosting in our classroom, dive-bombing over our heads for sport.

Kids screamed. I also wanted to scream — but I couldn't, I was the teacher.

We moved to the 3rd-floor classroom. The office staff looked at me like I was dramatic northerners, calmly picked up a net, and went to catch them. (In my defense — I'm a Taipei girl. Bat families in classrooms are simply not a thing up north.)

Day 2: The Blocked Domain

My classroom's URL was blocked by the education bureau's content filter. Dynamic DNS, they said.

One email. Whitelisted within minutes. I have never been so grateful to an office worker.

(Whoever answered that email — I owe you a cake.)

The Kids

They never even noticed the system had been swapped. They just kept adventuring.

  • They fought over level-ups, yelled over rare apron drops, and argued about whose team had more points: the younger kids fumed that the older kids were ahead; the older kids fumed when the younger ones overtook them on the very last day.
  • The price-guessing game? They were glued to their tablets. Guesses hit the big screen instantly, EXP flew, chaos was glorious.

The Food Day — the Best Day

We finally made our hand-made food dream happen:

  • 熱壓吐司 with 熟竹筍 + 玉米 + 鮪魚 — devoured in three minutes by a classmate's little boy.
  • 蕃薯 + 起司 — sweet, salty, dangerously good.
  • 珍珠糖鬆餅 so good we genuinely discussed quitting teaching to open a shop near the science park. (We're still teachers. For now.)

Around the Camp — Days 4 & 5 in Pictures

Sweet Moments I Still Don't Know How to Answer

  • A boy looked at me very seriously and said, “Teacher, you're pretty.” I pretended not to hear. (A girl said the same thing last camp. I was equally helpless both times. Thank you, kids, but I really don't know how to respond.)
  • They asked my age. “1985,” I said. They didn't believe me. “You can't check my ID — that's a police privilege. Become a police officer first.”
  • A few wanted to be my kid, or to introduce a boyfriend to me. “Calm down. I just want to be your teacher.”
  • They found and subscribed to my YouTube channel. (It exists only for the camp. I told them so.)
  • And on the last day — my birthday eve — they sang me Happy Birthday. I was so happy I bought drinks for my whole co-teaching team.

The Letters

The kids wrote letters to Little Oyster. We replied in character, as Little Oyster, sealing every letter with the memory of this summer.

Teaching is messy. Some weeks are bats, bugs, and burnout. And then a classroom of kids sings you a birthday song a day early — and you remember exactly why you chose this in the first place.

Some summers you just teach. This summer, I got to be part of the story. 🦪

#BilingualEducation #TeacherLife #SummerCamp #K12Education #Teaching #Tainan #EdTech
body.html_zh:
🏕️ 五天。一場雙語營。一家三口蝙蝠、一台充滿 bug 的備用伺服器，以及一整班孩子為我唱的生日快樂歌。

我剛結束在台南的第二場雙語夏令營。每個人都在問我辦得如何，所以這裡奉上最誠實無修飾的版本。

史上最慘烈的開局

開營前一晚，我發著燒，半夜 12 點半還在修改課堂遊戲化系統。我設了 5 點半的鬧鐘，結果實際醒來已經是 6 點 55 分。我一路狂奔衝向營隊，整個人狼狽得像剛被卡車撞過一樣——對早已在樓下苦等的同學一路狂道歉。

接著，伺服器掛了。就在那天早上。它跑在我朋友的電腦上，而他當時人在國外，救援得等到下午 4 點才能趕到。於是我們靠著一個充滿小 bug 的舊版本撐過第一天——剛好只夠記錄經驗值，外加大家彼此約定「千萬要記得按存檔」——然後我當晚親手救回了正式伺服器。隔天，所有數據紀錄無縫合併回去。

接著蝙蝠登場了

中午時分，一位學生拉開窗簾，赫然發現……黑黑的東西。一隻蝙蝠。接著兩隻。是一家三口的蝙蝠直接在我們教室築巢棲息，還把從我們頭頂俯衝當作娛樂運動。

孩子們放聲尖叫。我也很想跟著尖叫——但我不能，因為我是老師。

我們緊急遷徙到三樓教室。總務處同仁看著我，眼神彷彿在看大驚小怪的台北俗，隨後淡定拿起網子去抓蝙蝠。（容我為自己辯解一下——我是台北長大的女生，教室裡住著蝙蝠一家人在北部根本是天方夜譚好嗎！）

第 2 天：網域遭阻擋

我們課堂系統的網址被教育局的內容過濾器擋了下來。他們說是動態 DNS 的緣故。

一封信寄出，幾分鐘內火速列入白名單。我這輩子從未對行政同仁如此感恩戴德過。

（不管當天回信解鎖的是哪位承辦同仁——我欠你一個蛋糕。）

孩子們

他們甚至從頭到尾都沒察覺系統被掉包了。他們只是心無旁騖地繼續冒險。

  • 他們為了升級爭得不可開交，為稀有圍裙掉落放聲尖叫，為哪隊分數領先激烈爭辯：低年級氣惱高年級遙遙領先，高年級在最後一天被低年級逆轉超車時氣得跳腳。
  • 猜價遊戲呢？他們雙眼黏在平板上。猜測一出立刻同步登上大螢幕，經驗值漫天飛舞，場面混亂卻無比精彩。

美食日——最棒的一天

我們終於實現了手作美食的夢想：

  • 熱壓吐司搭配熟竹筍 ＋ 玉米 ＋ 鮪魚——同學家的小男孩三分鐘就狼吞虎嚥一掃而空。
  • 蕃薯 ＋ 起司——甜中帶鹹，好吃到令人上癮。
  • 珍珠糖鬆餅美味到我們全體認真討論要不要乾脆辭掉教職，去南科附近開家鬆餅店。（大家放心，目前我們還是老師啦。）

營隊剪影——第 4 天與第 5 天圖輯

那些我至今依然不知該如何接話的甜蜜瞬間

  • 一個小男生臉色非常認真地看著我說：「老師，你好漂亮。」我只能假裝沒聽到。（上一場營隊也有個小女生這樣說過，兩次我都一樣不知所措。謝謝孩子們，但我真的不知道該回什麼啊！）
  • 他們問我幾歲。「1985 年。」我說。他們打死不信。「你們不能看我的身分證——那是警察的特權，先去考上警察再說。」
  • 有幾個孩子吵著想當我的小孩，或是要幫我介紹男朋友。「冷靜點，我只想當你們的老師。」
  • 他們竟然搜出並訂閱了我的 YouTube 頻道。（我跟他們說那個頻道純粹是為了營隊教學存在的。）
  • 而在最後一天——正好是我生日前夕——他們全班為我唱起了生日快樂歌。我開心到直接請全體協同教學團隊喝飲料。

信件

孩子們寫信給小蚵人。我們以小蚵人的角色身分一一回覆，將這個夏天的所有回憶封存在每一封信中。

教書有時是一場兵荒馬亂。有些星期充滿了蝙蝠、軟體 bug 和精疲力竭。但接著，一整班的孩子提前一天為你唱起生日快樂歌——你瞬間又記起了自己當初為什麼選擇走上這條路。

有些夏天，你只是在教課。但今年夏天，我有幸成為了故事的一部分。🦪

cover.alt: From My First Conference Submission to Helping 11 Classmates Begin Theirs

body.html:
I still remember how uncertain I felt when I began preparing my first conference submission.

I did not know exactly what a conference abstract should contain. I was unsure how to turn a broad thesis direction into a smaller, manageable topic. I also did not know when I should approach my advisor, what materials I needed to prepare, or which parts of the process AI could genuinely support.

There was no single moment when everything suddenly became clear.

I learned by reading submission guidelines, studying official templates, organizing the data I already had, discussing possible directions with my advisor, experimenting with different AI tools, and checking the mistakes those tools made.

Slowly, an unfamiliar process became a sequence of steps I could understand.

After completing my own submission to a conference at Southern Taiwan University of Science and Technology, I began to wonder:

Could the path I had just walked become a map for someone else?

On July 31, I held an online sharing session for classmates who had never submitted to an academic conference before.

Excluding myself, 11 classmates joined the session.

The prepared presentation lasted approximately one hour, followed by another 40 minutes of questions and discussion.

This was not a lecture about asking AI to write a paper.

It was a conversation about how first-time researchers could move from uncertainty to action, while keeping academic judgment, research responsibility, and final decisions firmly in human hands.

Designing the Session for People Starting from Zero

I designed the session specifically for classmates with no previous conference submission experience.

I did not want to assume that everyone already understood academic publishing, research terminology, submission formats, or the relationship between an abstract, a full paper, and a conference presentation.

Instead, I organized the session around three practical questions:

How does conference submission actually work?
How can different AI tools support different stages of the process?
What is the smallest practical step someone can take today?

The session covered the complete journey from understanding a call for papers to preparing for submission.

I walked through official guidelines, submission forms, abstract structures, full-paper requirements, scheduling, oral presentations, and poster preparation.

I also explained how a larger thesis direction could be divided into a smaller conference topic, and why an advisor should remain involved in key academic decisions.

The goal was not to make conference submission look effortless.

The goal was to make the process visible.

When people can see what comes next, a large and unfamiliar task becomes less intimidating.

The First Step Is Not Asking AI to Write

One of the most important ideas I shared was that the first step should not be opening an AI tool and typing:

“Please write my conference paper.”

Before asking AI to produce anything, researchers need to understand what they already have and what remains uncertain.

What is the broader thesis direction?

What scores, student work, prompts, interviews, questionnaires, classroom records, or other materials are already available?

Which part of the larger research direction is small enough to address within the conference deadline?

Which decisions still require discussion with an advisor?

For first-time researchers, asking AI to generate an entire paper too early can create a dangerous illusion of progress.

The writing may appear complete, but the research question may still be unclear.

Missing evidence may be quietly replaced with invented details. Weak reasoning may be hidden behind polished academic language. References may look convincing without actually existing or supporting the claim.

I therefore encouraged everyone to begin with unknowns, evidence, and possible directions, rather than demanding a finished answer.

AI can help identify missing information, compare possible topics, organize existing materials, and prepare questions for discussion with an advisor.

However, it should not decide the research direction on the researcher’s behalf.

Five Models, Five Different Roles

Another major part of the session focused on the differences between AI models.

I did not want to turn this into a competition over which model was “the best.”

In practice, different models behave more like team members with different strengths, limitations, and working styles.

Based on my own experience:

  • GPT tends to consider many possibilities. It is useful for identifying logical gaps, suspicious citations, fabricated references, inconsistent claims, and unsupported interpretations.
  • Claude is strong at following templates, document requirements, and structural instructions. It is useful when working with official conference formats or planning academic posters.
  • Kimi can handle a wide range of tasks and longer documents, but users need time to understand its functions and learn how to prompt it effectively.
  • Grok responds quickly and is useful for brainstorming, exploring new directions, and generating ideas for images or multimedia.
  • Gemini feels conversational and integrates conveniently with Google’s ecosystem, but important academic content still requires careful verification because hallucinations may occur.

The purpose of this comparison was not to tell everyone which model they should pay for.

It was to introduce a more responsible question:

Which tool is suitable for this particular task—and who will verify its output?

One model may help organize materials. Another may be assigned to review weaknesses, unsupported claims, or suspicious references.

However, the final review of evidence, methods, interpretation, and citations must still be completed by the researcher and advisor.

AI can join the research team.

It should not quietly replace the researcher.

Using My Own Submission as a Transparent Example

I did not want the session to remain at the level of general advice.

I opened the actual submission guidelines, forms, abstract structure, research materials, and poster examples, and walked through the process step by step.

I also used my own conference submission as a transparent example.

My broader thesis direction involves cognitive scaffolding in generative AI image creation, student work, student prompts, and possible differences between general education students and students with special educational needs.

That full research direction was far too large for one conference abstract.

The submission therefore needed to focus on a smaller question that could be supported by the data I already had.

During the session, I showed both completed outputs and unfinished materials behind them: existing scores, student work, prompts, research notes, possible variables, statistical summaries, alternative research storylines, and the final abstract direction.

By showing the materials behind the finished product, I wanted participants to see that a conference paper is not created in a single leap.

It is assembled through a series of smaller decisions, each of which can be inspected, discussed, and revised.

AI assisted with organization, comparison, and formatting.

However, deciding which research storyline had sufficient evidence, which findings should be excluded, how limitations should be described, and how results should be interpreted remained human decisions.

I also emphasized one lesson that AI can easily oversimplify:

A statistically non-significant difference does not prove that two groups are completely identical.

Language matters in academic writing.

A result should not be made more dramatic simply because a stronger sentence sounds more impressive.

Turning Prompts into a Four-Level Scaffold

I knew that placing several prompts on presentation slides would not be enough.

Participants might take screenshots during the session and never return to them. Longer prompts are also inconvenient to copy from a slide.

I therefore created a supporting website where classmates could copy the prompts directly and continue using them after the meeting.

The website organizes the AI-assisted workflow into four levels.

Level 1: Clarify

Identify missing information, available materials, possible topics, risks, and decisions that still require discussion with the advisor.

At this stage, AI is not allowed to write the complete abstract.

Level 2: Structure

Use the official conference requirements and an evidence table to create an outline or a structured first draft.

Missing information must remain clearly marked as “to be confirmed,” rather than being filled in by AI.

Level 3: Review

Ask AI to act as a reviewer and identify missing evidence, methodological weaknesses, contradictions, excessive claims, and formatting risks.

The purpose is to reveal problems, not immediately rewrite everything into a polished version.

Level 4: Verify

Use another model to identify suspicious references, inconsistent numbers, unsupported statements, and possible hallucinations.

Then return to the original paper, database, PDF, data file, and advisor for human verification.

The four levels reflect a principle I strongly believe in:

The more complex the task, the more important it is to preserve visible checkpoints.

AI should not receive the raw materials and silently transform them into a finished paper.

There should be intermediate outputs that researchers can inspect, question, revise, and discuss with their advisors.

The prompts are not shortcuts around thinking.

They are scaffolds for thinking.

From a One-Hour Presentation to a Ten-Day Action Plan

I also wanted the session to end with something more useful than motivation.

“Start preparing your conference submission” is too vague.

It sounds important, but it does not tell someone what to do after closing the meeting window.

I therefore divided the process into a ten-day action plan:

  1. Download the official guidelines and submission form.
  2. Write the broader thesis direction in one sentence.
  3. List the data and materials currently available.
  4. Prepare several possible directions to discuss with the advisor.
  5. Compare candidate topics.
  6. Create an evidence table.
  7. Draft the main sections of the abstract.
  8. Conduct reverse review and cross-model verification.
  9. Revise the draft after receiving the advisor’s feedback.
  10. Complete the final formatting and submission checklist.

The first day is deliberately simple.

Participants do not need to understand everything immediately.

They only need to download the official documents and begin.

People are often not stopped because they are incapable of completing the entire project.

They are stopped by the belief that they must understand the entire project before taking the first step.

A useful scaffold does not remove the challenge.

It makes the next action visible.

The Discussion Became a Second Part of the Session

The prepared presentation lasted approximately one hour, but the session continued for another 40 minutes through questions and discussion.

That extended conversation was not something I had fully scripted in advance.

Because the participants were classmates, the atmosphere was relaxed. I did not read from a complete script. I followed the slides, opened real materials, and explained the process through examples from my own experience.

As the discussion continued, classmates gradually connected the framework to their own thesis ideas, available data, and concerns about working with an advisor.

Some questions were about AI tools, but many were more fundamental:

  • Is my current topic small enough for a conference submission?
  • Can the data I already have support a paper?
  • Should I prepare several possible directions before speaking with my advisor?
  • How much can AI organize before human judgment becomes necessary?
  • How do I move from an abstract to a full paper or poster?

The 40-minute discussion reminded me that first-time authors rarely struggle with only one technical step.

Their uncertainty often involves research direction, academic conventions, deadlines, advisor communication, and confidence at the same time.

The most useful thing I could offer was therefore not always a single correct answer.

Sometimes it was helping someone transform:

“I do not know what to do”

into:

“Here are the two or three things I need to confirm next.”

That shift may appear small, but it is often where action begins.

The Real Evaluation Comes After the Session

Around the middle of August, I plan to follow up with the classmates who attended.

I want to know:

  • Who has discussed a topic with an advisor?
  • Who has identified a manageable research question?
  • Who has begun drafting an abstract?
  • Which parts of the presentation or website were genuinely useful?
  • Where did people still become stuck?
  • Did anyone eventually complete a submission?

I do not want to assume that a well-prepared presentation automatically creates educational impact.

Attendance is only the beginning.

The more meaningful question is what happens after the meeting.

Did anyone take the first step?

Did the scaffold reduce uncertainty?

Did the prompts support thinking, or did they create new confusion?

Did the ten-day plan help participants move from intention to action?

The answers may help me improve the website, prompts, and future sharing sessions.

They may also become a later reflection on how to evaluate an educational sharing activity—not only by how many people attended, but by what participants were able to do afterward.

What I Took Away from the Experience

This was a small online sharing session with 11 classmates.

But to me, it represented something larger.

I had taken an experience that once felt confusing and personal, organized it into a process, and offered it back to others in a form they could use.

The presentation, AI model comparison, prompt website, and ten-day checklist were all tools.

The real purpose was simpler:

To make the first step easier to see.

AI can help us organize research, inspect weaknesses, compare possibilities, and work faster.

But it should not make the researcher disappear from the process.

The most valuable use of AI is not producing a finished academic paper with the fewest possible clicks.

It is helping people think more clearly while keeping evidence, responsibility, and judgment visible.

I hope this session will not remain only as something I completed.

I hope it becomes the beginning of someone else’s first conference submission.

我依然清楚記得，當初開始準備第一篇研討會投稿時，內心有多麼徬徨不安。

我不清楚研討會摘要到底該包含哪些要素；不知道如何把寬泛的論文大方向濃縮成精準聚焦的小主題；不知道該在什麼時間點找指導教授討論、需要先準備好什麼資料，更不清楚整個過程中到底哪些環節是 AI 可以真正提供實質協助的。

這條路上，從來沒有任何一個瞬間是突然茅塞頓開的。

我是透過逐字閱讀徵稿簡章、仔細研讀官方格式範本、整理手頭現有的數據資料、與指導教授反覆探討可行方向、親自實測各種 AI 工具，並逐一挑出工具犯下的錯誤，才一點一滴學會的。

漸漸地，一個原本完全陌生的歷程，轉化為一連串我能夠清晰理解與執行的具體步驟。

在順利完成自己向南臺科技大學研討會的投稿後，我開始思考：

我剛剛走過的這段路，能不能成為其他人前進的地圖？

7 月 31 日，我為從未有過研討會投稿經驗的同學舉辦了一場線上分享會。

扣除我自己，共有 11 位同學全程參與。

準備好的簡報分享了大約 1 個小時，隨後進行了長達 40 分鐘的提問與深度交流。

這絕不是一場教大家「如何叫 AI 幫你寫論文」的講座。

這是一場深度的對話：探討新手研究者如何從無所適從走向展開行動，同時將學術判斷、研究責任與最終裁決權牢牢掌握在研究者自己手中。

為零經驗的新手量身設計分享

我特別針對完全沒有研討會投稿經驗的同儕量身規劃了這場分享會。

我不想預先預設大家都已經理解學術出版生態、研究術語、投稿格式，或者摘要、全文與現場發表的對應關係。

相反地，我圍繞著三個極其實際的核心問題展開架構：

研討會投稿到底是如何運作的？
不同的 AI 工具該如何在各階段提供精準支援？
今天每個人可以踏出的最小、最切實的第一步是什麼？

整場分享涵蓋了從看懂徵稿啟事到最終備齊資料送出的完整旅程。

我帶領大家一步步檢視官方格式規定、投稿表單、摘要結構、全文規範、時程規劃、口頭發表技巧與學術海報製作要點。

我也詳細示範如何將龐大的畢業論文大題目拆解為適合研討會規模的精準題目，以及為什麼在所有關鍵學術決策上，指導教授都必須保持深度參與。

分享的目的絕不是要把研討會投稿粉飾得毫不費力。

我們的目標是讓整個流程「具象可見」。

當大家能清晰看見下一步該做什麼時，一項龐大而陌生的任務就不再令人望而生畏。

第一步不是叫 AI 開始寫

我分享的核心觀念之一就是：第一步絕對不該是打開 AI 視窗輸入：

「請幫我寫一篇研討會論文。」

在要求 AI 產出任何內容之前，研究者必須先清楚盤點自己已經掌握了什麼，以及還有哪些關鍵尚未釐清。

更寬廣的論文大方向是什麼？

手邊已經有哪些現成的測驗成績、學生作品、提示詞紀錄、訪談逐字稿、問卷數據、課堂觀察筆記或其他一手素材？

大題目中哪一部分足夠聚焦，能在研討會截稿期限前順利完成？

哪些關鍵決策仍然必須先與指導教授確認？

對於初次涉足研究的人來說，過早要求 AI 生成整篇論文，容易營造出一種危險的「進度假象」。

文章表面上看起來結構完整，但核心研究問題可能依然含糊不清。

缺失的證據可能被 AI 悄悄以捏造的細節填補；薄弱的邏輯推論可能被優雅的學術辭藻掩飾；參考文獻看起來極具說服力，實際上卻根本不存在，或完全不支援該項主張。

因此，我因此鼓勵大家從「未知、證據與可行方向」著手梳理，而不是急著索求一份現成的標準答案。

AI 可以協助挑出資訊缺口、評估候選主題、整理現有素材，並為與指導教授的討論預備好精準的提問清單。

但是，它絕不能越俎代庖替研究者決定研究的核心方向。

五大模型，五種不同角色

分享會的另一個重點聚焦於不同 AI 模型之間的特質差異。

我不想把這個環節變成「哪一款模型最強」的無謂評比。

在真實的研究工作流中，不同的模型更像是一支各懷絕技的團隊成員，擁有各自的優勢、極限與工作風格。

基於我自己的實務經驗：

  • GPT 傾向於全面考量多種可能性。非常適合用來挑出邏輯漏洞、抓出可疑引文、揪出偽造文獻、檢驗前後矛盾的主張，以及標記缺乏證據支撐的過度推論。
  • Claude 擅長嚴格遵循範本規格、格式要求與層級結構指令。在套用官方研討會排版格式或規劃學術海報版面時極為得力。
  • Kimi 能夠處理多樣化的任務與長篇文檔，但使用者需要花時間熟悉其功能並掌握高效的提問技巧。
  • Grok 反應敏捷迅速，非常適合用來腦力激盪、探索全新視角，以及發想視覺圖像或多媒體創意。
  • Gemini 語氣自然親切，且能便利整合 Google 生態圈；但面對學術關鍵內容仍須極度嚴謹查證，防範模型幻覺產生的錯誤。

這項對比的目的，不是為了向大家推銷該花錢訂閱哪一款。

而是引導大家提出一個更具研究責任感的提問：

哪一個工具適合這項特定任務——而最終由誰來核實它的產出？

我們可以指派一個模型協助梳理資料，再委派另一個模型專門審查薄弱環節、無證據的主張或可疑文獻。

然而，針對證據、方法、研究詮釋與引文字句的最終把關，依然必須由研究者本人與指導教授親自完成。

AI 可以加入研究團隊。

但它絕不能悄悄取代研究者本人的主體性。

以我自己的投稿作為完全透明的範例

我不希望這場分享僅停留在泛泛的空談建議。

我直接打開真實的投稿簡章、表單、摘要架構、研究原始資料與海報範本，一步步拆解示範。

我也將自己向南臺科大研討會投稿的真實過程，當作完全透明的示範案例。

我的大論文研究方向涵蓋生成式 AI 圖像創作中的認知鷹架、學生實作作品、學生提示詞，以及普通班學生與特教學生的可能差異。

如此龐大的研究版圖，顯然遠遠超出單篇研討會摘要所能承載的容量。

因此，該篇投稿必須聚焦於一個手頭已有完整數據支撐的精巧子問題。

在分享會中，我同時展示了最終定稿與其背後尚未加工的半成品：現有評量成績、學生作品、提示詞紀錄、研究札記、候選變項、統計摘要表、不同的研究故事線架構，以及最終拍板的摘要方向。

透過完整攤開成品背後的這些基石，我希望讓大家看見：一篇研討會論文從來不是一蹴可幾的飛躍。

它是由一連串微小的決策逐步拼裝而成，而每一個決策都是可以被檢視、討論與修正的。

AI 在整理、比對與格式排版上提供了協助。

然而，裁決哪條研究故事線具備足夠證據力、哪些發現該果斷割捨、研究限制該如何嚴謹描述，以及結果應當如何客觀詮釋，始終屬於人類的專業判斷。

我也特別強調了一個 AI 極易過度簡化的學術常識：

統計上未達顯著差異，並不等於兩組對象完全一模一樣。

在學術寫作中，精準的字句至關重要。

我們絕不能僅僅因為更強烈的句子聽起來更具震撼力，就擅自將研究結果戲劇化誇大。

將提示詞化為四層階梯式鷹架

我很清楚，光把幾段提示詞貼在簡報投影片上是遠遠不夠的。

聽眾可能在當下截圖存檔，之後卻再也沒有打開過；而且冗長複雜的提示詞要從投影片上一字字複製也非常不便。

因此，我特地搭建了一個專屬支援網站，讓同學們能直接一鍵複製提示詞，並在會後持續實際運用。

這個網站將 AI 輔助的研究工作流梳理為清晰的四個層級：

Level 1：釐清（Clarify）

梳理缺失資訊、現有素材、潛在主題、研究風險，以及哪些關鍵決策必須優先與指導教授討論。

在此階段，嚴格禁止要求 AI 直接撰寫完整摘要。

Level 2：架構（Structure）

依據官方研討會規範與現有證據表，搭建出大綱或結構化的第一版草稿。

所有尚未確定的缺失資訊，必須明確標註為「待確認」，絕不允許 AI 隨意腦補填空。

Level 3：審查（Review）

要求 AI 化身嚴苛的匿名審查員，揪出證據漏洞、方法學瑕疵、邏輯矛盾、誇大主張與格式排版風險。

目的在於指出問題，而不是立刻把文章潤飾成看似完美的表面文章。

Level 4：查證（Verify）

指派另一套模型專門抓取可疑引文、矛盾數據、無依據論述與潛在幻覺。

最後，研究者必須親自回歸原始論文、資料庫、PDF、數據檔案與指導教授端，完成嚴密的人工核實。

這四個層次體現了我深信不疑的核心原則：

任務越複雜，保留清晰可見的檢查點就越發關鍵。

AI 不該在收下原始素材後，暗箱操作直接變出一篇現成論文。

中間必須具備清晰的中介產出，讓研究者能夠親自檢查、質疑、修改，並與指導教授深入研討。

提示詞不是用來繞過思考的捷徑。

它們是輔助思考的鷹架。

從一小時的分享，到十天的行動計畫

我希望這場分享會的結尾，能帶給大家比心靈雞湯更具體有用的東西。

「開始準備你的研討會投稿吧」這句話太過空洞。

它聽起來無比崇高，卻完全無法告訴大家關掉會議視窗後的下一秒到底該做什麼。

因此，我將整個歷程細分為具體的十日行動計畫：

  1. 下載官方徵稿簡章與投稿專用表單。
  2. 用一句話清楚寫下論文大方向。
  3. 具體盤點目前現有的數據與手頭素材。
  4. 準備幾個可行方向與指導教授初步討論。
  5. 評估比較候選主題。
  6. 建立研究證據對照表。
  7. 起草摘要各核心段落初稿。
  8. 進行反向審查與跨模型交叉查驗。
  9. 依據指導教授的回饋意見修改精鍊初稿。
  10. 完成最終格式排版與投稿檢查清單確認。

第一天的任務被刻意設計得無比簡單。

大家不需要一開始就掌握所有全局。

大家只需要下載官方文件，然後踏出那一步。

人們之所以停滯不前，往往不是因為缺乏完成整件事的能力。

而是被一種誤解所困住：誤以為自己必須先想通整件事的所有細節，才配邁出第一步。

真正有用的教學鷹架並非幫你消滅挑戰。

而是讓下一步的行動變得清晰可見。

討論環節成為分享會不可或缺的下半場

預先準備的簡報進行了大約 1 個小時，但整個會議藉由熱烈的提問與討論持續了整整 40 分鐘。

這段深入的交流並非我事先排練好的劇本。

因為與會的都是同儕同學，氣氛輕鬆而真誠。我沒有照本宣科念講稿，而是順著投影片展開真實素材，結合自己親身走過的經驗逐一剖析。

隨著討論推進，同學們逐漸將這套框架與自己構思的論文主題、現有資料，以及如何與指導教授溝通的焦慮連結在一起。

有些問題圍繞著 AI 工具，但更多問題回歸到了最本質的研究層面：

  • 我目前的題目足夠小、適合投研討會嗎？
  • 手邊現有的資料足以支撐起一篇論文嗎？
  • 在跟指導教授約談之前，我需要先準備好幾個可能方向嗎？
  • 在必須由人類專業判斷介入之前，AI 最多可以先幫我整理到什麼程度？
  • 從一篇摘要要如何順利拓展成全文或壁報發表？

這 40 分鐘的討論深刻提醒了我：初次接觸研究的新人，面臨的困境往往從來不只是單純某個技術環節。

他們的迷惘往往同時交織著研究方向、學術慣例、截稿壓力、指導教授溝通以及自信心等多重維度。

因此，我能提供最有價值的協助，往往不是給出一個標準答案。

有時只是陪伴他們把心態從：

「我完全不知道該怎麼辦」

轉化為：

「這是我接下來需要確認的兩三件具體事情。」

這個轉變看似微小，但這正是所有實質行動萌芽的起點。

真正的成效檢驗在分享會落幕之後

8 月中旬左右，我計畫逐一關心與會的同學們。

我很想了解：

  • 誰已經與指導教授討論過題目了？
  • 誰已經鎖定了切實可行的研究問題？
  • 誰已經開始動手撰寫摘要初稿？
  • 分享會或提示詞網站的哪些內容發揮了真正實質的幫助？
  • 大家在哪些環節依然容易卡關？
  • 是否有人最終順利完成了投稿？

我不想理所當然地認定一場精心準備的分享就必然會產生教學影響力。

出席人數僅僅是起點。

更有意義的考驗在於會議結束後真實發生的改變。

是否有人真正邁出了第一步？

這套鷹架是否切實減輕了不安？

這些提示詞是啟發了思考，還是帶來了新的困惑？

十日計畫是否真正幫助大家把意圖轉化為行動？

這些答案將指引我進一步優化網站、改進提示詞與未來的分享活動。

它們也將轉化為日後評估一場教育分享成效的深層省思——評估的指標不僅是有多少人參與，更是大家在會後真正做成了什麼。

這段歷程帶給我的深刻收穫

這只是一場與 11 位同儕參與的精緻線上分享會。

但對我而言，它代表著更宏大的意涵。

我把一段曾經令自己困惑、獨自摸索的個人經歷，有系統地整理成標準流程，並以具體可用的形式回饋給身邊的人。

簡報、AI 模型對比、提示詞網站與十日檢核清單都只是工具。

真正的初衷其實非常純粹：

讓第一步變得清晰可見。

AI 可以協助我們梳理研究、檢驗瑕疵、比對可能性並加速產出。

但它絕不該讓研究者本人的身影在整個歷程中淡出。

AI 最有價值的用法，絕非用最少的手指點擊生成出一篇現成的學術論文。

而是幫助大家更清晰地思考，同時讓證據、責任與學術判斷清晰可辨。

我期盼這場分享會不只是一件被我標記為「已完成」的工作。

我期盼它能成為其他人第一次研討會投稿的美好開端。

title.en: From One Month to Two Days: Rebuilding My K–12 SUNO Scaffolding Website with Kimi
title.zh: 從一個月到兩天：用 Kimi 重構我的 K–12 SUNO 提示詞鷹架網站

summary.en: In 2024, I spent nearly a month working with Gemini and Google Sites to build a SUNO lyric-prompt scaffolding website for my students.
summary.zh: 2024 年，我花了將近一個月的時間，結合 Gemini 與 Google 協作平台，為學生搭建了一套 SUNO 歌詞提示詞鷹架網站。

cover.alt: From One Month to Two Days: Rebuilding My K–12 SUNO Scaffolding Website with Kimi

body.html:
In 2024, I spent nearly a month working with Gemini and Google Sites to build a SUNO lyric-prompt scaffolding website for my students.

At the time, I was proud that I had managed to turn an idea into something students could actually use.

But once the website entered the classroom, the students taught me something that code alone could not:

A tool can work perfectly and still feel difficult to use.

The original website contained the learning content I wanted. It offered themes, subtopics, rhyme options, musical styles, and a structure for turning feelings and ideas into lyric prompts.

However, the interface placed a long theme list beside an equally long form. Some students were unsure where to begin, what to select next, or how the different sections were connected.

On a desktop, it was manageable.

On a phone or tablet, it became much less intuitive.

Recently, while preparing a new educational website for a teaching design competition, I found myself looking back at this older project.

The new competition website was built entirely from zero to one, but because it is my main submission, I cannot share it publicly yet.

The SUNO website is not currently being submitted, so I decided to revisit it first.

Not because the old version had failed—but because the students’ experience had already shown me how it could become better.

And I was also curious about something else:

Could a terminal-based AI improve the UI and UX of an existing website without the kind of live visual preview we usually rely on?

That question became my two-day experiment with Kimi.

Day 1: Letting Kimi Code Work from the Terminal

I began with Kimi Code in the terminal.

Instead of rebuilding everything from scratch, I let it inspect the existing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, theme data, and interaction logic.

My goal was to preserve the original instructional structure while improving the way students moved through it.

The website still needed to help students:

  • find a theme that felt meaningful;
  • describe the story or emotion they wanted to express;
  • choose rhyme patterns, performers, and musical styles;
  • assemble a complete prompt; and
  • bring that prompt into a lyric model and then SUNO.

What needed to change was not the educational purpose.

It was the experience of reaching it.

The most interesting part was seeing how Kimi Code compensated for the lack of a continuous live preview.

It generated multiple screenshots while testing the website—desktop pages, mobile layouts, the theme library, selected states, pop-ups, panels, and other interaction views.

When I opened the project folder, I found an entire row of preview images.

It felt almost as though the terminal had created its own way of “looking” at the interface.

This workflow also felt different from using a traditional chat interface.

In my experience, it was more economical with tokens because Kimi could work directly inside the project rather than repeatedly regenerating and explaining large sections of code.

I could also interrupt at any time, add another issue, or place a new task into the queue while it was still working.

I did not always have to wait for one complete response before continuing the conversation.

That made the process feel less like submitting one request at a time—and more like working beside someone while continuously adding notes to the task board.

Still, the limitation was obvious.

Even with screenshots, visual communication was not as immediate as seeing the page update directly in front of me.

Day 2: Returning to Kimi Chat for the Mobile Experience

On the second day, I returned to Kimi Chat.

The terminal had already completed much of the structural and visual work, but detailed mobile UI adjustments were still easier when I could compare my screenshots with the preview more directly.

This stage focused mainly on the phone and tablet experience.

I marked specific problems in screenshots and explained what felt difficult:

  • text becoming too light after selecting a main theme;
  • buttons that were not clear or touch-friendly enough;
  • long pages that made students lose track of the next step;
  • navigation controls that needed to remain accessible on smaller screens; and
  • visual states that did not make the student’s current choice obvious enough.

These details may appear small, but in a K–12 classroom, they matter.

A student who cannot immediately tell whether a button has been selected may stop and ask the teacher.

A student who cannot find the next step may assume they have done something wrong.

A student using a phone should not have to fight the interface before they can begin creating.

The revised website therefore reorganized the experience into three clearer stages:

Find Inspiration → Build the Prompt → Turn It into a Song

The original teaching structure remained largely intact.

What changed was the path through it.

Instead of presenting a large amount of information at once, the redesigned version tries to guide students through one meaningful decision at a time.

From a Project Folder to a Live Website

After the revisions were complete, I asked Kimi to prepare the entire website as a deployable ZIP file.

I did not need to manually organize the files or build the deployment package myself.

Kimi generated the ZIP for me. I only needed to download it and upload the complete file to Netlify.

The website was then ready to go live.

That part of the process was unexpectedly convenient.

For someone working on educational tools rather than managing a complicated software deployment pipeline, removing those final technical steps makes a real difference.

The result is now a responsive static website that works across desktop, tablet, and mobile.

🔗 Live website: https://suno-scaffold.netlify.app/

Two Days Did Not Replace the Original Month

It would be tempting to describe this as:

“AI helped me replace one month of work with two days.”

But I do not think that is the real story.

Those two days were only possible because the original month had already happened.

The 2024 website gave me a starting point.

The classroom gave me evidence.

The students gave me the questions I had failed to anticipate while designing alone.

Without watching them hesitate, search for buttons, or become unsure about the next step, I would not have known what to ask Kimi to improve.

AI accelerated the implementation.

But the students revealed what was worth changing.

UX Is Also a Form of Scaffolding

This project reminded me that instructional scaffolding does not exist only in lesson plans, worksheets, sentence starters, or teacher explanations.

It also exists in interfaces.

A readable button is scaffolding.

A visible next step is scaffolding.

A mobile layout that does not interrupt a student’s train of thought is scaffolding.

When students spend less energy trying to understand the tool, they can spend more energy expressing what they actually want to create.

That is why I no longer see UI and UX as decoration added after the educational content is finished.

For K–12 learners, the interface is part of the teaching.

The terminal workflow still has limitations, especially around visual feedback and live preview.

However, after completing this project, I learned how to ask the terminal to launch a local offline preview once the website is ready.

A friend has also developed a tool that can capture screenshots and pass the visual results directly back to a terminal-based AI.

These additions may solve much of the visual gap.

That will probably become my next experiment—and another story to share later.

For now, this redesign left me with one thought:

AI may help us build faster, but our learners still show us what deserves to be built better.

body.html_zh:
2024 年，我花了將近一個月的時間，結合 Gemini 與 Google 協作平台，為學生搭建了一套 SUNO 歌詞提示詞鷹架網站。

那時候，我很自豪自己成功把一個想法轉化為學生真正能夠在課堂上使用的工具。

但是，當這個網站真正進入真實教室後，學生們教會了我一段純靠寫程式永遠學不會的道理：

一個工具即使功能運作完全正常，用起來依然可能讓人感到吃力挫折。

最初的網站確實涵蓋了我想要的所有教學內容：提供了創作主題、子題、押韻選項、音樂風格，以及將心緒感受與靈感轉化為歌詞提示詞的完整架構。

然而，介面上卻是把一份長長的主題清單，直接擺在另一份同樣冗長的表單旁邊。有些學生根本不知道該從哪裡開始、下一步該點什麼，或者各個區塊之間到底有什麼關聯。

在桌上型電腦的大螢幕上，勉強還能應付。

但一換到手機或平板上，整個體驗立刻變得極不直覺。

最近，在為一場教學設計競賽準備全新教育網站的過程中，我不知不覺回頭審視起這個早期的老專案。

參賽的新網站完全是從零到一重新打造的，但因為它是我的主要參賽作品，目前還不能對外公開發布。

而這個 SUNO 網站目前沒有參賽限制，於是我決定先回過頭來重新打磨它。

並不是因為舊版本失敗了——而是因為學生們過去的真實使用經驗，早已為我指明了它能變得多棒的方向。

而且，我心中也對另一件事充滿了好奇：

一個運行在終端機裡的 AI，在缺乏我們平時習慣的即時視覺預覽的情況下，是否真能有效改善現有網站的 UI 與 UX？

這個疑問，催生了我與 Kimi 展開的這場為期兩天的實戰實驗。

第 1 天：讓 Kimi Code 在終端機裡動工

我從終端機裡的 Kimi Code 起步。

我沒有推倒一切從零重寫，而是讓它直接盤點現有的 HTML、CSS、JavaScript、主題資料以及互動邏輯。

我的目標是在完整保留原始教學架構的同時，大幅改善學生在各步驟之間的探索流暢度。

網站依然必須持續引導學生：

  • 找到讓自己心有共鳴的創作主題；
  • 具體描述想要表達的故事或情感；
  • 選擇押韻模式、演唱者設定與音樂曲風；
  • 組裝出結構完整的提示詞；以及
  • 將該提示詞帶入歌詞生成模型，進而輸入 SUNO 產出歌曲。

需要改變的，從來不是教育初衷。

而是抵達這個目標的體驗過程。

整個過程最有趣的發現，是看著 Kimi Code 如何自行克服缺乏連續即時視覺預覽的限制。

在測試網站期間，它主動生成了大量螢幕截圖——桌機版面、行動裝置版型、主題庫瀏覽、選中狀態、彈出視窗、抽屜面板以及其他互動視圖。

當我打開專案資料夾時，赫然看見一整排整整齊齊的預覽截圖。

那種感覺，就像終端機自己摸索出了一套專屬於它「看懂」視覺介面的獨特方式。

這樣的工作流程與使用傳統對話介面有著截然不同的感受。

在我的實際體驗中，這樣做更加節省 token 額度，因為 Kimi 能直接在專案內部穿梭改檔，而不需要反覆在對話框中重新輸出並長篇大論解釋整段整段的程式碼。

我也能隨時中途打斷、補充新的問題，或者在它持續作業的同時把新任務排進等待佇列。

我不再需要苦苦等待一條完整回覆結束才能進行下一輪對話。

這讓整個過程不像是在一次次提交孤立的提示詞——更像是在工作檯邊並肩作戰，同時持續在任務看板上追加便條紙。

當然，它的侷限性同樣非常明顯。

即使有自動截圖，視覺層面的溝通依然無法比得上直接看著網頁在眼前即時動態更新來得直覺順暢。

第 2 天：重返 Kimi Chat 打磨行動端體驗

到了第二天，我切換回 Kimi Chat 介面。

終端機已經完成了大部分的架構搭建與視覺雛形，但針對手機與平板的細緻 UI 微調，在能夠將截圖與預覽效果直接對照的情況下，推進起來還是更為高效。

這個階段幾乎全神貫注在手機與平板的操作體驗上。

我直接在截圖上圈出具體問題，詳細說明哪裡讓人感到卡頓不適：

  • 點選主要主題後，文字對比度過低變得看不清楚；
  • 按鈕不夠清晰直覺，且不夠方便觸控點擊；
  • 頁面太長，導致學生滑著滑著就迷失了下一步在哪裡；
  • 在小螢幕上，導覽控制項目必須保持清晰易用；以及
  • 選取狀態不夠醒目，無法讓學生一眼看清當前選擇。

這些細節看似微不足道，但在中小學的真實課堂上，每一個細節都舉足輕重。

一位學生只要無法在第一時間確定按鈕到底有沒有被選中，就會停下動作轉頭問老師。

一位學生只要找不到下一步該點哪裡，就會下意識以為自己是不是做錯了什麼。

拿著手機學習的孩子，不應該在開始動手創作之前，先花費力氣跟笨拙的介面搏鬥。

因此，改版後的網站將整體流程重新梳理為三個清爽無比的階段：

尋找靈感 → 構建提示詞 → 化為歌曲

原本的教學核心骨幹幾乎完整保留了下來。

徹底改變的，是穿梭其間的旅程。

新版本不再把排山倒海的資訊一次性砸在學生眼前，而是試圖引導孩子們一次只專注做好一個有意義的創作決定。

從專案資料夾直達正式上線網站

所有修改調整完畢後，我請 Kimi 直接將整個網站打包成一份可立即部署的 ZIP 壓縮檔。

我完全不需要自己手動整理歸納檔案，也不必親自配置繁瑣的打包建置流程。

Kimi 為我一鍵生成了 ZIP 包。我唯一需要做的，就是把它下載下來，整包上傳到 Netlify。

整個網站瞬間就準備好正式向全世界發布了。

這個環節的流暢度完全超乎我的預期。

對於專注於開發教學工具、而非專職維運複雜軟體部署管線的教育者來說，能省去最後這幾步棘手的技術門檻，真的帶來了巨大的解脫。

現在的成品是一個兼顧桌機、平板與手機的響應式靜態網站。

🔗 正式上線網站： https://suno-scaffold.netlify.app/

兩天的重構，從未取代最初的那一個月

人們很容易忍不住這樣描述這段經歷：

「AI 幫我把原本要花一個月的工作，縮短成短短兩天就做完了。」

但我認為，這並非故事的真實全貌。

那兩天的爆發，之所以能夠成真，純粹是因為最初那一個月的辛苦探索早已真切地發生過。

2024 年的舊版網站為我奠定了出發的基石。

真實的教室給了我無可取代的實證反饋。

而學生們，給了我當初獨自閉門設計時永遠料想不到的關鍵提問。

如果沒有親眼看著孩子們在螢幕前猶豫遲疑、到處找按鈕，或者在面對下一步時一臉茫然，我根本無從得知該指揮 Kimi 去改進什麼。

AI 大幅加速了落實的速度。

但真正揭示出「什麼值得被改得更好」的，始終是學生。

使用者體驗（UX），本身就是一種教學鷹架

這個專案再次提醒了我：教學鷹架（scaffolding）並不僅僅存在於教案手冊、學習單、引導句型或老師的口頭講解之中。

它同樣深刻地烙印在使用者介面（UI）裡。

一顆清晰好讀的按鈕，是鷹架。

一個清晰可見的下一步引導，是鷹架。

一個不會打斷學生創作思緒的手機版面配置，更是實實在在的鷹架。

當學生能省下摸索工具的認知負荷時，他們就能把更多的精力傾注在表達自己真正想要創造的內容上。

這也是為什麼我不再把 UI 與 UX 視為教學內容完成後才隨意貼上的點綴裝飾。

對 K–12 的學習者來說，介面本身就是教學不可分割的一環。

終端機工作流目前依然有其侷限，特別是在缺乏即時視覺反饋與連續動態預覽的部分。

不過，在完成這個專案之後，我也學會了如何在網站就緒後要求終端機直接啟動本機離線預覽。

而且一位朋友最近也開發了一款小工具，能自動抓取截圖並將視覺結果直接回傳給終端機裡的 AI。

這些新工具的加入，很可能會大幅弭平大部分的視覺落差。

那大概會成為我下一階段的實驗目標——也是日後可以再跟大家分享的新故事。

就目前而言，這次的重構留給了我深刻的感觸：

AI 或許能幫助我們打造得更快，但永遠是我們的學習者，為我們指明什麼才真正值得被建造得更好。

body.html:
This is the story of everything in between — because my cross-disciplinary portfolio is officially live!

I've compiled my journey from physical fashion design to GenAI web development and K-12 EdTech applications into one central hub: “Measure with Reason, Name with Poetry.”

This website was designed with the concept of a “Starry Art Gallery.” As you navigate through it, you'll encounter portraits of women from different eras and artistic movements — from children to the elderly. They represent the different stages and facets of my soul: the “old soul” perspective that gives me gravity, beautifully balanced by a straightforward, pure, and sincere heart.

Many people ask how a fashion design background led to teaching IT, building GenAI web apps, and conducting academic research. The truth is, none of these skills were acquired overnight. They are the result of a lifelong obsession with the “0 to 1” creation process:

🎹 Age 7: My mom decided I should learn piano — and literally had one carried up to our apartment. My dad, seeing it as a waste of money, had the movers take it right back down. (No regrets though — I probably wouldn't have become a concert pianist anyway! 😂)

✍️ Age 9: Hooked by The Saga of Darren Shan, I began writing my very first novel — and yes, I still keep the handwritten notes!

💻 Age 10–11: Took my first steps into web design using Dreamweaver.

🎵 Age 11–12: Forcibly drafted into the school choir by my teacher, I gritted my teeth through two full years of vocal training — never imagining it would quietly resurface, years later, in how I compose and refine songs with SUNO. By junior high, I was already slicing audio in GoldWave — a tool still on active duty in my production pipeline today.

📜 Age 12–13: Discovered Photoshop (CS2/CS3). Finding it challenging at first, I treated it like an online MMO, following internet tutorials until I mastered it.

👺 Age 13–14: Deep into the Pili Puppetry fandom during the golden age of Wretch (無名小站). I self-taught CSS and HTML to design custom styles and mouse cursors for my fellow fans. That same year, I joined the school computer club. As the only girl in a room full of boys, I found the introductory C++ agonizingly dry, so I promptly defected to the printmaking club instead!

🦅 Age 14–15: Penned classical Chinese poetry, including the piece “The Long Song (江湖難)” featured in the portfolio.

📖 Age 16: Secured an A-level publishing contract with QiDian for a long-form novel. I also spent that summer pouring my energy into writing a 200,000-word manuscript instead of preparing for university entrance exams. The result? My exam scores tanked completely, and I ended up in Fashion Design — a serendipitous accident that sparked a whole new chapter.

🎶 Age 16–17: Wrote a full set of classical Chinese lyrics and hummed an original melody for a xianxia novel I was writing, though I had no way to produce it at the time.

🎭 Age 16–17 (cont.): Totally immersed in cosplay. On a shoestring budget, I even cut and styled my own wigs to save money. I navigated a top-tier high school in Taipei with a mix of street smarts and a bit of rule-bending — staying on such good terms with the strict military instructors that running bento errands for them became my licensed excuse to slip out the school gates for drinks and snacks.

🧵 Age 18–19: As destiny would have it, I entered Fashion Design at Fu Jen Catholic University. (Chinese Literature — a mentor talked me out of it, probably worried the discipline would smother my creativity 😂. Drama — I'd dreamed of screenwriting. Information Communication — all of it rewritten by that summer's exam results.) I was completely lost and uninspired in my freshman year. But then, something mysterious clicked during my sophomore year. Sitting at the sewing machine, I suddenly fell into a state of deep, meditative focus — and out of nowhere, the craft of draping, pattern-making, and sewing just flowed as if it were an innate gift. I even won an award at the university's Fashion Week.

🏆 Age 22: Clinched 1st place in the graduation exhibition. Moving into graduate school, I channeled this intense focus into academic research, eventually graduating at the top of my class with the President's Award.

🕸️ Age 26: Long before GenAI, I self-taught no-code web architecture (Wix) to build a high-traffic information platform and strategy hub for a mobile gaming community. I later handed it over to others due to my busy schedule — though I refuse to claim responsibility for their subsequent “aesthetic downgrades”! 😜

🎮 The Unlisted Chapters: And for the unlisted chapters in between? Let's just say that between managing a long-term health “boss fight” and leading some highly successful (but strictly classified) “0 to 1” creative side quests, my life has never actually had a blank page. Some chapters are just reserved for the expansion pack. 😉

🧠 The Methodology (Recent): People often ask how I learn things so fast without formal training or cram schools. The truth is, I don't just study; I build systems to decode the chaos. For example, I built a custom Gemini Gem to analyze my weak spots and utilized Google AI Studio TTS to generate tailored listening tracks, boosting my TOEIC score from an old 605 to 695 in exactly one month. My core strength isn't just acquiring skills; it's extracting methodologies from the chaos — so that “talent” stops being the price of admission to extraordinary results.

The transition into tech and AI wasn't a sudden pivot. I was deeply researching early GenAI music tools and GPT-3.5 back when they first launched, long before they became mainstream waves.

In fact, when SUNO was released, it finally gave me back that virtual piano my dad sent away. I fed my high school melody and lyrics into it, bringing a long-held dream to life.

🎵 “Liao Zhai (寥哉)” — Short MV Preview

玉晶綴珠釵

Jade hairpins adorn her crown,

暾日映紅腮

As the rising sun blushes her cheeks red.

情愛 就像雲靄消散開來

Love, like mist, dissolves into the air,

烏雲成了阻礙

Left only with dark clouds that bar the way.

(These lines open on female lead wedding day — jade hairpins and dawn-blushed cheeks, a bride marrying the God-King to save her brother; the dissolving mist and gathering clouds already foretell a love heaven will not allow.)

A word about the name: “Liao Zhai (寥哉)” is a homophonic play on Pu Songling's classic “Liaozhai Zhiyi (聊齋誌異)” — but where his strange tales haunt the mortal world, mine is a xianxia saga of gods, demons, and a love that breaks heaven's law. 寥哉 itself is a classical sigh — “how desolate” — and it closes my novel's own prologue: “the souls fall silent, the realms go still — one can only sigh: liao zai.” The short story took 2nd place in a high-school writing contest; the full-length novel, and these lyrics, grew from it.

If the vocals in the short MV below sound a little too “human” for a typical AI track... well, let's just say some secrets are better left in the void. 🤐✨

Every skill — whether it's code, fabric, pedagogy, or prompt engineering — shares the same DNA: the drive to build something magnificent from nothing.

Even Illustrator, which I avoided for years, was conquered out of absolute necessity. During a uniform design commission for Fu Jen Catholic University Hospital, I gave myself just one month to self-learn the software to draft complex technical garment drawings. It ultimately earned praise from the most notoriously critical, sharp-tongued professor in our department. 😂

🔗 Explore the Portfolio here: https://echoofwren.github.io/portfolio/

P.S. Yes, my connection count is intentionally lean. I curate a highly focused, high-ROI network rather than chasing vanity metrics. But if you are a fellow developer, architect, or creator who loves breaking down and rebuilding systems as much as I do — don't let the small number deter you. 😉

Feel free to scan the QR codes on my newly deployed banner to explore a more casual, everyday side of my journey on Instagram (where I recently completed a random real-world social experiment), or drop a direct line to my inbox. Let's see what happens when the right nodes finally connect. 🚀✨

這是這段歲月裡所有故事的交織——因為我的跨領域作品集正式上線了！

我將自己從實體服裝設計、生成式 AI 網頁開發到 K–12 教育科技實踐的完整歷程，匯整進這個核心樞紐：「以理度量，以詩命名」（Measure with Reason, Name with Poetry）。

這個網站以「星空美術館」為概念打造。漫步其中，你將邂逅跨越不同時代與藝術流派的女性肖像——從孩童到年邁長者。她們象徵著我靈魂在不同階段的多元切面：既有賦予我沉穩重量的「老靈魂」視角，又與一顆純粹、率真而熾熱的赤子之心完美交融。

許多人常問，一個服裝設計背景的人，究竟是如何跨界教起資訊科技、打造生成式 AI 網頁應用，並投入學術研究的？坦白說，這些技能沒有一項是一夕促成的。它們全源於我一生對「從 0 到 1」創作歷程的極致著迷：

🎹 7 歲：媽媽決定讓我學鋼琴——真的請搬琴師傅把一台鋼琴一路扛上了我們家公寓。我爸覺得這純粹是浪費錢，當場叫搬家師傅原車搬下樓。（不過沒什麼好遺憾的——反正我也成不了鋼琴演奏家啦！😂）

✍️ 9 歲：被《向達倫大冒險》深深著迷，動筆寫下了人生第一部長篇小說——沒錯，當年的手寫草稿我至今還好好收著！

💻 10–11 歲：用 Dreamweaver 踏出了網頁設計的第一步。

🎵 11–12 歲：被老師強行抓進學校合唱團，咬牙硬撐過整整兩年的發聲訓練——萬萬沒料到這段經驗，竟在多年後我用 SUNO 譜曲與微調歌曲時悄然回魂。到了國中，我已經在用 GoldWave 剪接音訊了——這款工具如今依然活躍在我的音訊製作工作流中。

📜 12–13 歲：接觸了 Photoshop（CS2/CS3）。一開始覺得難如登天，我把它當成線上遊戲打怪破關，跟著網路教學一步步摸索直到徹底駕馭。

👺 13–14 歲：無名小站全盛時期，深陷霹靂布袋戲同人圈。為了替廣大戲迷設計個人專屬樣式與滑鼠游標，我自學了 CSS 與 HTML。同年加入學校電腦社，作為滿屋子男生中唯一的女生，我發現入門 C++ 枯燥得令人抓狂，於是果斷叛逃到了版畫社！

🦅 14–15 歲：提筆創作古典詩詞，包括作品集中收錄的那首〈江湖難〉。

📖 16 歲：長篇小說斬獲起點中文網 A 級簽約合約。那個夏天，我把所有精力都傾注在寫下一部二十萬字的原稿上，完全把大學升學考試拋在腦後。結果呢？聯考成績徹底大爆死，意外掉進了輔大織品服裝系——這場美麗的意外，卻為我開啟了全新的人生篇章。

🎶 16–17 歲：為自己創作的仙俠小說譜寫了一整首古風歌詞，並親自哼唱出原創旋律，雖然當時的我根本沒有任何專業設備能把它製作出來。

🎭 16–17 歲（續）：徹底沉迷 Cosplay。在有限的預算下，連假髮都是自己動手剪裁造型來省錢。在台北一所頂尖高中就讀期間，我靠著一點街頭智慧和靈活遊走於規則邊緣的手腕適應校園生活——跟嚴格的教官打好關係，幫忙跑腿買便當成了我能光明正大溜出校門買飲料和點心的合法藉口。

🧵 18–19 歲：命中注定般，我進入了輔仁大學織品服裝學系。（中文系——曾被導師勸退，大概是擔心嚴謹的學科會扼殺我的創作野性 😂；戲劇系——我曾夢想當編劇；資傳系——全都在那個夏天的聯考成績單下被改寫）。大一時我無比迷惘，找不到靈感。但到了大二，奇蹟般的事情發生了。坐在縫紉機前，我突然進入了一種極致寧靜的冥想心流狀態——立體剪裁、打版、車縫工藝宛如天賦本能般流淌而出，我甚至在輔大織品服裝週拿下了獎項。

🏆 22 歲：一舉奪下畢業展第一名。進入研究所後，我將這股極度專注的狂熱投入學術研究，最終以第一名榮獲 President's Award 畢業。

🕸️ 26 歲：早在生成式 AI 出現之前，我便自學 No-Code 網頁架構（Wix），為手遊社群打造了一個高流量的資訊平台與攻略核心。後來因個人行程忙碌移交給他人維護——不過他們後續把網站「審美降級」，我可概不認帳喔！😜

🎮 未列出的章節：至於這段歲月中那些未列出的空白？只能說，在一邊與長期健康的「大 Boss」搏鬥、一邊帶領幾場極為成功（但嚴格保密）的「從 0 到 1」創意支線任務之間，我的人生其實從未有過真正的空白頁。有些章節，純粹是留給未來的資料片再公開。😉

🧠 方法論（近期）：常有人問我，在沒有科班背景或補習的情況下，究竟是如何如此快速掌握新技能的？事實上，我不只是在學習；我是在建立系統來「解碼混亂」。舉例來說，我自己打造了專屬的 Gemini Gem 來剖析個人弱點，並運用 Google AI Studio 的 TTS 生成量身定做的聽力音檔，在短短一個月內將我的多益成績從早年的 605 分衝上了 695 分。我的核心優勢從來不只是獲取技能，而是從混亂中提煉出方法論——讓「天賦」不再是通往非凡成果的高不可攀門檻。

跨足科技與 AI 絕非突發奇想的轉彎。早在生成式 AI 音樂工具與 GPT-3.5 剛問世之初，在它們成為大眾風口之前，我就已經在深度研究探索了。

事實上，當 SUNO 推出時，它終於將當年被爸爸退回去的那台虛擬鋼琴重新交還到了我手中。我把高中的原創旋律與歌詞餵進系統，讓擱置多年的夢想鮮活成真。

🎵 〈寥哉〉——短版 MV 預告

玉晶綴珠釵

Jade hairpins adorn her crown,

暾日映紅腮

As the rising sun blushes her cheeks red.

情愛 就像雲靄消散開來

Love, like mist, dissolves into the air,

烏雲成了阻礙

Left only with dark clouds that bar the way.

（這幾句詞揭開了女主角的大婚之日——珠釵綴髮、晨曦映頰，一位為了拯救兄長而嫁予神王的待嫁新娘；消散的雲靄與聚攏的烏雲，早已預示了一段不容於天地的逆天之戀。）

關於歌名的小由來：〈寥哉〉諧音取自蒲松齡的經典《聊齋誌異》——然而不同於他的狐鬼異事徘徊人間，我的故事是一場神魔交鋒、逆天抗命的仙俠史詩。「寥哉」本身是一聲古雅的喟嘆——意為「何其寂寥冷清」——它亦落筆於我小說本身的序卷終句（譯意：「群生俱寂，萬境皆默——唯有一嘆：寥哉」）。這部短篇曾榮獲高中校園文學獎第二名；而後來的長篇小說與這闕歌詞，皆由此孕育而生。

如果底下短版 MV 中的人聲聽起來比一般的 AI 音軌多了一絲過於真實的「人味」……嗯，有些秘密就讓它留在虛空之中吧。🤐✨

每一項技能——無論是程式碼、布料布匹、教學法，還是提示詞工程——都流淌著相同的基因：那股在虛無之中從零造出壯麗事物的熾熱渴望。

就連我曾排斥多年的 Illustrator，最終也在絕對的現實需求下被徹底攻克。在承接輔仁大學附設醫院的制服設計專案期間，我硬是給自己一個月期限自學軟體，畫出極其複雜精密的服裝工業技術規格圖。最終，這份作品贏得了我們系上出了名最挑剔、說話最狠辣的教授盛讚。😂

body.html:
Our bilingual camp came to a smooth close on July 10th. A typhoon crashed the party midway and forced us to condense part of the program — but watching the kids stay fully, joyfully immersed all the same, I felt a relief and warmth I can hardly put into words.

This camp handed me a whole string of life "firsts": not only my first time ever attending a camp, but my first time daring to serve as its overall coordinator. Before this, my only "lead" experience was back at the Graduate Institute of Textiles & Clothing at Fu Jen Catholic University — an eleventh-hour assignment from the department chair to coordinate the runway show for an alumni banquet.

So I'd be lying if I said I wasn't nervous. This camp marked my return to the classroom after a year away (my last teaching post was at a junior high school), and my return to an elementary school setting after two full years. In the days before camp, I was quietly restless — frantically squeezing lesson prep and rehearsal into every spare scrap of time, terrified of slipping up somewhere.

To raise the stakes further, the opening and closing ceremonies fell to me and one experienced teammate. My head held exactly one thought: do not drag the team down. Host well. Stay calm!

Thankfully, both ceremonies landed far better than I expected. Several teammates even praised me as a natural host (but believe me — this was the first time in my life I'd ever held a hosting mic). Maybe some strange dormant switch got flipped! Drawing on a lifetime of stage training — class president duties, running class meetings, speech contests — plus a packed May of academic conferences, my heartbeat somehow, miraculously, steadied the instant I stepped on stage. Words flowed; I could actually set the whole room alight.

Honestly, this camp was only the "second" bilingual teaching experience of my life. The first was during my junior-high teaching days: to pass a classroom-English certification, I had to rehearse with my students again and again before I dared film the certification video. This time, facing a room of children under twelve, I somehow delivered fully bilingual lessons to kids in rural Tainan without the luxury of thorough rehearsal — a version of myself even I never saw coming.

Throughout the camp preparations — advising professors, camp teammates, the coordinating teachers at both schools — nearly everyone watching me work carried the same question mark in their minds:

"If you're this capable, why aren't you in tech or textiles making far more money? Why become a schoolteacher?"

Since I formally moved into education, this question has played on loop like background music. Industry seniors thought walking away from fashion design was a waste of my craft; professors figured that with the Fu Jen Textiles halo, I'd shine far more easily out in industry; friends, knowing my combined strengths in information technology, saw my not pivoting to tech as talent plainly squandered.

But let me say this openly: choosing education was never an impulsive or careless decision. It is woven inseparably into the story of my whole life.

I was never a healthy child. As an infant I developed what Taiwanese folk call "stinky head" — scalp ringworm — which took a long, long time to cure. In my final year of kindergarten, severe pneumonia put me in the hospital for a full seven days, and I missed my own kindergarten graduation. As if under some curse, nearly every stage of my schooling came bundled with a major illness; "in and out of hospitals" became one of the defining memories of my youth. Perhaps that is also why, now that I stand in classrooms myself, I find myself caring far more stubbornly about my students' physical and mental wellbeing than about their grades.

The other memory that has deeply shaped my life's decisions: at every stage of school, I was lucky enough to meet a teacher capable of turning my life's direction. Each of them pointed to the unfinished parts of me, and led me, step by step, closer to a whole version of myself.

Looking back at my working life: aside from two two-month industry internships in textiles and fashion during my Fu Jen years, and a brief stint as a product designer in my first year of grad school, my center of gravity has always orbited "education".

My first part-time job in college was caring for the young children of immigrant spouses attending the university's continuing-education school, staying with them until classes ended. In grad school I worked as a TA, coaching undergraduates through exhibitions and runway shows, grading their draping assignments and reports. The truth is, I had been quietly working in education all along — my blueprint at the time was simply a different route: study abroad for a PhD in fashion design, then return to teach at Fu Jen.

That's also why I threw myself into major projects like the uniform design commission for Fu Jen Catholic University Hospital, and kept close, warm ties with the founding sisters and professors of the department — because back then, I genuinely longed to pass everything I'd learned about fashion design on to the students who would come after me.

Then fate played an enormous joke on me.

At 23, I collapsed into illness — and with that one blow, the road abroad, the PhD, all of it, was gone.

I still remember it with perfect clarity: the doctor looking at 24-year-old me across the consultation desk and saying, gravely, "Once you begin biologic treatment, it may truly be very difficult for you to ever carry a child…" In that instant — to say it didn't hurt would be a lie. It isn't that my womb is impaired; it's that biologics and immunosuppressants severely affect fetal development. To prepare for pregnancy, I would have to stop my medication for at least a year — and the moment I stop, my merciless RP would launch its assault on my body all over again. The condition I fought so hard to stabilize would spiral out of control, and could very well take my life.

This, without question, was fate's ultimate test for me.

But life has never been a single-answer question, and the road ahead is never just one path. Medicine's progress gave me a second chance at life; fate took away my ability to bring new life into the world in the flesh —

So why not turn the question around: I can use my knowledge to nurture the next generation of lives!

The pivotal people in my life have always been bound to education. I may not be able to serve in the halls of higher education for now — but I can pass my life's lessons and knowledge on to these children, holding nothing back, the way the teachers who once lit my way did for me, and spark something different in their lives.

Perhaps, in this lifetime, I am destined never to have a child who carries my own blood. But in my two years on the front lines of education, I have already gathered nearly 600 children — nurtured, deeply, with my knowledge and my heart.

And that number will only keep growing.

Speaking of these children, allow me to share two pieces of "user feedback" I will treasure for the rest of my life — and both happened within these five short days of camp:

On clay-crafting day, a little girl named Mila — about to enter second grade — ran up to me, pressed a clay heart ring she had made with her own hands into mine, and said, with the most earnest eyes: "Teacher, you are so beautiful." As someone hopeless at accepting compliments, all I could do was awkwardly pat her head and stammer that the Strawberry Bear on her shirt was very cute too 😅. But in that heart-warming instant, I knew with absolute certainty — this is why I choose to stay in education.

Another student, a senior grader named Olivia, gave me a little capybara charm. I happily pinned it straight onto my everyday bag, because it perfectly captures my current philosophy of life: stay calm, stay grounded, and keep going with the flow 🦦✨.

Devoting myself to education — spending three whole extra years as a teacher-training student just to become an elementary school teacher — must look, to anyone chasing returns, like a thankless job with terrible ROI. Everyone says "your choices matter more than your effort"; between teacher and engineer, the engineer certainly earns far more.

But I insist on telling the children, from my own lived experience — and on cheering for every colleague still quietly gritting their teeth in a classroom somewhere:

Money matters, truly. But life is long, and some things no amount of money can ever buy.

I count myself lucky to be a member of the "Hot-Blooded Fools Club", gladly doing this exhausting, thankless work. My reasoning is simple: every great scientist, statesperson, physician, and business titan in this world — which of them was not shaped and awakened by education? And now I have the honor of standing shoulder to shoulder with teachers everywhere, nurturing these lives of boundless possibility — with education.

The old saying goes, "the student surpasses the master." I genuinely cannot wait for these children to spread their wings and become the legends who lead human progress. In the long journey of their lives, I may be nothing more than the briefest flicker of memory; but as long as I can help them even a little, I will gladly keep digging into this soil called education. That is also why I keep pushing for innovation, weaving EdTech into my classroom — because I want to give every last bit of the best future I can offer to these children.

Finally, allow me to close this journey with a video full of laughter. By Day 3 of camp, the kids had already, quietly, taught themselves the theme song I wrote for them. This clip captures the final day — everyone off the stage, going wonderfully wild, singing and dancing their hearts out —

That said — as the self-appointed Ultimate Dance Disaster, I not only mixed up left and right during the sing-along, I botched several key moves in a row 😂. But watching the kids laugh, sing, and not care one bit about perfection — that was the happiest, most healing moment of my entire camp. Sometimes you really do need to shed the tight armor of the "expert" and be gloriously silly for the kids. Why not?

Day 2 | Five-Senses Vocabulary, Blooket & Water-Filter STEAM

Day 3 | Banquet Culture & BINGO

Day 4 | Menu Design, Clay Food & the Closing Ceremony

我們的雙語營在 7 月 10 日圓滿落幕。雖然中途颱風攪局不得不壓縮部分活動，但看著孩子們依然全情投入、笑聲不斷，我心中湧現一股難以言喻的欣慰與溫暖。

這個營隊送給了我一連串人生的「第一次」：不僅是我這輩子第一次參加營隊，更是第一次大膽挑大樑擔任營隊總召。在此之前，我唯一的「總策劃」經驗，還得追溯到輔仁大學織品服裝研究所時期——系主任在最後一刻指派我統籌系友餐會的時尚伸展台走秀。

所以如果說我不緊張，那絕對是騙人的。這個營隊標誌著我睽違一年後重返講台（我上一份教職是在國中），也是睽違整整兩年再度踏進國小校園。在開營前的日子裡，我內心充滿了隱秘的焦慮——瘋狂抓緊每一絲零碎時間備課與反覆排練，深怕自己在哪個環節漏了拍子。

更讓壓力倍增的是，開閉幕典禮的主持重任落在了我和另一位經驗豐富的隊友肩上。我腦袋裡當時只有一個念頭：絕對不能拖累團隊。一定要主持好，保持冷靜！

謝天謝地，兩場典禮的表現遠遠超出了我的預期。甚至好幾位隊友誇獎我是天生的主持人（但相信我——這是我這輩子第一次握著主持麥克風）。也許是我體內某個沉睡的神秘開關被悄悄打開了！仰賴著從小到大積累的舞台訓練——當班長、主持班會、參加演講比賽——加上五月份剛跑完一整個月密集的高壓學術研討會發表，奇蹟似地，當我踏上舞台的那一秒，心跳瞬間穩定了下來。字句自然流淌，我甚至能夠點燃全場的熱情。

老實說，這場營隊也僅僅是我人生中「第二次」雙語教學實戰。第一次是在國中任教期間：為了通過課堂英語認證，我跟學生在台下一遍又一遍排練，才敢開機錄製認證影片。這一次，面對滿室未滿十二歲的孩子，我竟然能夠在缺乏充分排練的情況下，在台南偏鄉小學從容自如地給孩子們帶來全雙語課程——連我自己都未曾預料到自己能展現出這樣的面貌。

在整個營隊籌備期間——指導教授、營隊夥伴、兩校的協同行政老師——幾乎所有看著我工作的人，心中都浮現著同一個大大的問號：

「你能力這麼好，為什麼不去科技業或紡織業賺大錢？為什麼偏偏要跑來當學校老師？」

自從我正式跨入教育領域以來，這個問題就如同背景音樂般在身邊無限循環播放。業界前輩覺得我離開服裝設計是糟蹋了手藝；教授們認為頂著輔大織品的光環，我在業界顯然能更輕易發光發熱；朋友們知道我跨足資訊科技的能力，認為我不轉行投入科技業簡直是暴殄天物。

但請容我坦率直言：選擇教育，從來不是一場一時衝動或輕率的決定。它早已密不可分地交織進我整個生命的軌跡之中。

我從小就不是個健康的孩子。嬰兒時期我就得了台灣民間俗稱的「臭頭爛耳」——嚴重的頭皮癬——花了極其漫長的時間才痊癒。在幼稚園大班那年，一場嚴重的肺炎讓我整整住院了七天，甚至因此缺席了自己的幼稚園畢業典禮。宛如某種揮之不去的宿命，我求學的每一個階段幾乎都伴隨著一場大病；「進出醫院」成了我青春歲月裡最深刻的印記之一。或許正因如此，如今當我自己站上講台時，比起冷冰冰的成績分數，我發現自己更加固執地在乎著學生身心的安好與健康。

另一段深深形塑我人生抉擇的記憶是：在求學的每一個階段，我都無比幸運地遇見了足以扭轉我人生方向的恩師。他們每一位都看見了我身上未竟的潛能，一步一步引領著我，走向更完整的自己。

回顧我的工作經歷：除了在輔大期間於紡織服裝業界實習過兩個月，以及研一短暫擔任過一陣子產品設計師之外，我生命的重心始終緊緊圍繞著「教育」旋轉。

我大學的第一份兼職，就是在進修推廣部照顧新住民配偶的小孩，陪伴他們直到家長下課。在研究所期間，我擔任助教，輔導大學部學弟妹籌備畢業展與走秀，批改他們的立裁作業與專題報告。事實上，我一直都在教育領域默默耕耘——只不過當時心中的藍圖是另一條路徑：出國攻讀服裝設計博士，然後回到輔大任教。

這也是為什麼當年我全力以赴承接輔仁大學附設醫院制服設計標案這類重大專案，並與系上的創辦修女及教授們保持著親密深厚的情誼——因為那時候的我，發自內心地渴望將自己在服裝設計上所學的一切，毫無保留地傳承給未來的學弟妹。

然而，命運跟我開了一個巨大的玩笑。

23 歲那年，我的身體轟然倒下——那一記重擊，讓出國深造、攻讀博士的所有夢想，瞬間化為泡影。

我至今依然記憶猶新：醫師坐在診間桌子對面，看著 24 歲的我，面色凝重地說：「一旦開始使用生物製劑，妳這輩子可能真的很難再有自己的孩子了……」在那一瞬間——說不心痛絕對是謊言。並不是我的子宮有任何損傷，而是生物製劑與免疫抑制劑會對胎兒發育造成極為嚴重的威脅。如果要備孕，我必須停藥至少一年以上——而一旦停藥，殘酷的復發性多軟骨炎（RP）將再度肆虐我的全身。好不容易穩定下來的病情將徹底失控，隨時可能奪走我的性命。

這毫無疑問是命運給我最極限的試煉。

但人生從來不是單選題，未來的路也從來不只有一條。醫學的進步賦予了我第二次生命；命運雖然剝奪了我透過肉身孕育新生命的可能——

那我何不把問題倒過來看：我可以用自己的知識，去孕育下一代的生命！

改變我人生的關鍵人物，始終與教育緊緊相繫。我現在或許無法登上高等學術殿堂執教——但我可以像當年為我提燈引路的老師們一樣，將我一生的所學與知識毫無保留地傳承給這些孩子，在他們的生命中點燃不一樣的光芒。

也許這輩子，我注定不會擁有帶有自己血緣的孩子。但在教育第一線耕耘的這兩年裡，我已經累積陪伴了近 600 位孩子——以我的知識與真心，深深地澆灌著他們。

而這個數字，只會繼續不斷增長。

說到這些孩子，請容我分享兩則我將珍藏一生的「使用者回饋」——而且它們全發生在這短短五天的營隊之中：

在黏土手作日那天，一位即將升上二年級、名叫 Mila 的小女孩跑向我，將她親手捏製的黏土愛心戒指塞進我的手心，眼神無比真摯地看著我說：「老師，你好漂亮。」作為一個極度不擅長接受讚美的人，我當時能做的只有手足無措地摸摸她的頭，結結巴巴地回她說她衣服上的草莓熊也很可愛 😅。但在那個溫暖心扉的瞬間，我無比篤定地確信——這就是我選擇留在教育界的理由。

另一位高年級的學生 Olivia，送給了我一個水豚小吊飾。我欣喜地直接把它別在我的隨身包上，因為它完美契合了我當前的人生哲學：保持冷靜、腳踏實地、順勢而為 🦦✨。

投身教育——甘願多花整整三年修習師資培育課程，只為了成為一名國小合格教師——在任何只看投報率的人眼裡，肯定像是一份吃力不討好的苦差事。大家都說「選擇比努力更重要」；在老師與工程師之間，工程師的薪水顯然豐厚得多。

但我堅持用自己的生命歷程告訴孩子們——也為每一位依然在某間教室裡默默咬牙堅守的教育同行喝采：

金錢確實很重要。但生命很長，有些珍貴的事物是再多金錢也永遠買不到的。

我很慶幸自己能成為「熱血笨蛋俱樂部」的一員，甘之如飴地做著這份疲憊卻神聖的工作。我的道理很簡單：這世界上每一位偉大的科學家、政治家、醫師與商業巨擘——哪一位不是被教育所塑造、所啟蒙喚醒的？而如今我有幸能與各地的老師們並肩站在一起，以教育孕育這些擁有無限可能的生命。

俗話說「青出於藍而勝於藍」。我由衷迫不及待想看著這些孩子展翅高飛，成為引領人類文明進步的傳奇人物。在他們漫長的人生旅途中，我也許不過是一抹轉瞬即逝的微小記憶；但只要能對他們帶來哪怕一點點的幫助，我就甘願繼續深耕這片名為教育的土壤。這也是為什麼我始終堅持推動教學創新、將教育科技融入課堂——因為我想將我所能給予的最好的未來，毫無保留地送到這些孩子眼前。

最後，請容我用一段充滿歡笑的影片為這趟旅程作結。到了營隊第 3 天，孩子們早已悄悄學會了我為他們寫的主題曲。這段影片記錄了最後一天——所有人衝下舞台，肆意歡笑，全心全意地又唱又跳——

話說回來——作為自封的「終極肢體殘障代表」，在帶唱跳時我不僅左右不分，還接連跳錯了好幾個關鍵舞步 😂。但看著孩子們大笑、高唱，絲毫不在意完不完美——那是整場營隊最令我快樂、最療癒的時刻。有時候，你真的需要卸下「專家」那層緊繃的盔甲，為了孩子們徹底耍寶一次。何樂而不為呢？

活動圖輯

感謝我溫暖熱心的隊友們捕捉下這些珍貴瞬間：

第 1 天 ｜ 勇士覺醒

body.html:
🎬 Theme Song MV: https://youtu.be/57aTGix7GQo

🔗 Explore All Tools Here: https://nb41f002.github.io/oyster-camp/

“What if camp administration could simply... disappear — so teachers could pour every ounce of energy into the kids?”

That was the question I kept asking myself when I took on my first-ever role as overall coordinator of 【Legend of the Little Oyster: The Green Chopstick Uprising (小蚵人傳說：綠竹筷的逆襲)】— a five-day bilingual summer camp for elementary students, running at Longgang Elementary in July and Baoxi Elementary in August, with about 30 campers per school.

Planning began back in March. From May onward, our team met every Monday evening — hammering out curriculum, site surveys, rosters, role assignments, even a full typhoon contingency plan with parent notification letters (this is southern Taiwan in summer, after all). As coordinator, I ran the meetings, kept the minutes, tracked every action item, and led the Baoxi site. I quickly learned that a camp isn't lesson plans — it's a hundred small administrative tasks that quietly devour a teacher's energy.

So instead of enduring the friction, I decided to design it away. Today — Day 3 of camp, with the kids already humming our theme song — I want to share the full journey.


🎲 World-Building: A Curriculum That Runs Entirely on TRPG

Here is the core of our design: the entire curriculum is built on a tabletop RPG (TRPG) framework. It's not decoration layered on top of English lessons — it IS the lesson structure. Every class is a quest, every learning goal is a mission objective, and every teacher plays an in-story character for the full five days, staying in role from morning circle to closing ceremony.

The storyline: the Little Oysters summon young heroes to defend the flavors of their hometown against the Golden Spoon Royal Chef — a proud, tsundere palace cook who refuses to believe humble Tainan dishes could rival his cuisine. Campers train, craft, and perform across five days, building toward a final storytelling showdown where the Royal Chef admits defeat at last.

Character & World Design (Gemini): I designed all five NPCs with Gemini for the artwork, iterating through multiple full redesigns until the visual style felt cohesive. Each character doubles as a real teaching role — the Guild Master anchors ceremonies and dispatches quests; the Golden Spoon Royal Chef drives the dramatic tension; the Master Chef Heir leads clay miniature food crafting; the Food Hunter runs experiments and music segments; and the Order Judge keeps the adventure on track with live, positive-only point scoring.

Campers are sorted into two guilds by grade band — the Fresh Oyster Heroes (lower & middle grades) and the Bamboo Shoot Heroes (upper grades). Every activity is designed once, then differentiated: extra scaffolding for the younger guild, extension challenges for the older one.

🛠️ The Camp-Ops Toolkit: Six Web Tools to Delete the Admin

Where it started: a beautiful but static paper schedule. Every revision meant reprinting, and nobody could ever be sure which version was current.

To give my teammates their evenings back, I independently developed a suite of six web tools — all lightweight, single-file static pages hosted free on GitHub Pages, zero dependencies, running on any phone:

📅 Student & Parent Schedule — RPG-styled and fully responsive; tap any class block to reveal detailed content. Always the latest version.

👩🏫 Teacher Schedule — instructor view with lead/support assignments, four-class switching, and award criteria at a glance.

✨ Prep Practice Station — every lesson's bilingual scripts, classroom callouts, and visuals in one place, with dark/light mode. Rehearse on the bus, or at midnight.

🪪 ID Card Generator — batch-produce camper badges in minutes instead of an evening in Word.

🎓 Certificate Generator — personalized completion certificates in a few clicks; every camper walks the stage, every team wins an award.

🎯 Mission Dispatch Board — daily staff assignments, transparent to the whole team.

Lesson-Plan Co-pilots (Custom GPT & Gemini Gem): Because bilingual lesson planning is the single biggest time sink, I also built a Custom GPT and a Gemini Gem pre-loaded with our camp's teaching framework — so every teammate drafts consistent, grade-differentiated bilingual lesson plans instead of starting from a blank page.

🎵 Engineering an Earworm: The Theme Song Pipeline

Composition & Prompt Iteration (SUNO): I wanted the kids to internalize our four classroom commands — not memorize them, but feel them. So I composed “Hero's Awakening” in SUNO, iterating on prompts and lyrics again and again to engineer a deliberate bilingual structure: Mandarin verses carry the story, an English pre-chorus name-drops the NPC heroes (“Food Hunter, look and see! Master Chef, cook with me!”), and a repeated, chant-like chorus is built entirely from the four commands.

MV Production (Gemini, Premiere Pro & Subtitle Edit): I storyboarded a 15-scene music video with Gemini, edited it in Premiere Pro, and fine-tuned the subtitles in Subtitle Edit.

The result? By Day 3, every camper responds instantly:

“Little Oysters!” → “Listen!” 👂  |  “Green Chopsticks!” → “Go!” ✊

“Golden Spoon!” → “Freeze!” 🥄  |  “Save the table!” → “Now!” 🍽️

When a lesson becomes a quest, English becomes the spell. 🪄

📈 The Road Ahead

●Running the second camp week at Baoxi Elementary in August — refining every tool based on this week's field data.

●Open-sourcing the toolkit on GitHub so other camp organizers can fork and adapt it.

●Expanding the Custom GPT / Gem with more differentiated lesson templates.

🙏 Acknowledgments & Call to Action

A heartfelt thank you to my teammates — who stayed in character for five days straight, choreographed the dance moves that brought the theme song to life, and trusted a first-time coordinator's slightly crazy idea of running a camp like a TRPG campaign. Watching a classroom of kids sing and dance to a song we made together is a feeling I won't forget. 😭

「如果營隊行政能直接……消失——讓老師能把百分之百的心力，毫無保留地傾注在孩子身上，那會是什麼模樣？」

這是我初次挑大樑接下【小蚵人傳說：綠竹筷的逆襲】營隊總召時，不斷反覆自問的核心問題——這是一場為期五天的小學生雙語夏令營，七月在龍崗國小、八月在保西國小舉行，每校約有 30 位營隊學童。

籌備工作早在三月就悄悄起跑。從五月開始，我們團隊每逢週一晚間定期開會——敲定課程架構、場地現勘、名冊分組、角色分配，甚至連完整的颱風應變計畫與家長通知單都一應俱全（畢竟這是盛夏的南台灣）。作為總召，我主持會議、撰寫會議記錄、追蹤每一項待辦事項，並帶領保西校區。我很快就體會到，辦營隊絕不只是寫教案——而是一百件微小繁瑣的行政雜務，在無聲無息中榨乾老師的精力。

因此，與其忍受這些繁瑣摩擦，我決定用設計讓它們徹底消失。今天——營隊第 3 天，當聽見孩子們已經在走廊輕聲哼唱我們的主題曲時——我想完整分享這趟旅程。


🎲 世界觀構建：完全架構在 TRPG 之上的全方位課程

這是我們設計的核心本質：整套課程直接建構在桌上角色扮演遊戲（TRPG）框架之上。它絕非硬套在英語課表外的膚淺點綴——它「就是」課程結構本身。每一堂課都是一個冒險任務，每一個學習目標都是一個通關任務，而每位老師都在整整五天中化身為故事裡的特定角色，從晨會到閉幕典禮始終沉浸在角色設定中。

故事主線：小蚵人召喚年輕勇士，挺身守護家鄉的美味記憶，對抗傲慢傲嬌的金湯匙總鋪師——一位堅信平民台南小吃根本不配與宮廷料理相提並論的御廚。小學童們在五天中不斷特訓、手作與展演，一路推進至最後的說故事大決戰，最終讓總鋪師甘拜下風。

角色與世界觀設計（Gemini）：我運用 Gemini 繪製了全體五位 NPC 的角色視覺，經歷了數次全套風格重構迭代，直到整體視覺風格融洽統一。每個角色同時兼具真實的教學職責——公會長坐鎮典禮與發布每日任務；金湯匙總鋪師營造全劇戲劇張力；傳奇總鋪師傳人負責黏土微縮美食手作；尋味獵人帶領實驗與音樂環節；而秩序審判官則透過即時、純加分機制的記分系統維持冒險秩序。

營隊學童依年段分屬兩大公會——鮮蚵勇士（低中年級）與綠竹筍勇士（高年級）。每項活動只需設計一次，隨後進行差異化分層：為年輕公會提供額外的教學鷹架支援，為高年級公會設計拓展挑戰任務。

🛠️ 營隊維運工具箱：六大網頁工具徹底消滅行政負擔

起點是這樣的：一張排版精美卻毫無彈性的紙本課表。每一次改動都意味著重新列印，而且沒有人能百分之百確定自己手上的是不是最新版本。

為了把寶貴的夜晚時間還給隊友們，我自主獨立開發了一整套共六個網頁工具——全部是輕量、單一檔案的靜態網頁，免費託管在 GitHub Pages 上，零外部相依性，任何手機能隨開隨用：

📅 學生與家長課表——充滿 RPG 遊戲風格且完全自適應響應；點擊任一課堂區塊即可展開查看詳細內容。永遠呈現最新版本。

👩🏫 教師課表——專屬講師視角，清楚標記主講／協同分工、四班快速切換，評獎標準一目了然。

✨ 備課練習站——將每堂課的雙語講稿、課堂呼應口令與視覺圖表匯整於一處，支援深色／淺色模式切換。無論在公車上還是半夜躺在床上都能隨時練習。

🪪 識別證鍛造爐——幾分鐘內批次生成全體學童的精美名牌，告別在 Word 裡熬夜排版的夢魘。

🎓 結業證書鍛造爐——點擊幾下即可批次產出個人化結業證書；讓每一位學童都能風光走上舞台領獎，人人皆有所獲。

🎯 任務派遣看板——每日人力崗位分工，對全體團隊透明公開。

雙語教案副駕駛（Custom GPT 與 Gemini Gem）：由於雙語教案編寫是最大的時間黑洞，我打造了一款預載我們營隊教學架構的 Custom GPT 與 Gemini Gem——讓每位夥伴都能產出格式一致、分層適性的雙語教案，無須面對白紙發愁。

🎵 打造洗腦神曲：主題曲研發管線

創作與提示詞反覆迭代（SUNO）：我希望孩子們能自然內化我們的四大課堂口令——不是死記硬背，而是深刻感受。於是我在 SUNO 中譜寫了〈勇士的覺醒〉，反覆微調提示詞與歌詞，精心設計出一套精準的雙語結構：中文主歌推進故事主線，英文導歌逐一點名 NPC 英雄（「Food Hunter, look and see! Master Chef, cook with me!」），而洗腦且具號召力的副歌，則完全由四大課堂口令所構成。

MV 後製剪輯（Gemini、Premiere Pro 與 Subtitle Edit）：我使用 Gemini 繪製了包含 15 個分鏡場景的完整音樂錄影帶分鏡腳本，在 Premiere Pro 中進行剪輯，並利用 Subtitle Edit 精確校準每一格字幕軸。

成效如何？到了營隊第 3 天，每位學童都能秒速直覺反射：

「小蚵人！」→「聽！」👂  |  「綠竹筷！」→「衝！」✊

「金湯匙！」→「定！」🥄  |  「救餐桌！」→「行！」🍽️

當一堂課化為一場冒險任務，英語便成為了最強大的魔法咒語。🪄

📈 未來展望

● 八月於保西國小展開第二梯次營隊——根據本週的現場實戰數據持續最佳化所有工具。

● 將整套營隊維運工具箱在 GitHub 上開源，讓更多營隊主辦者能夠自由 Fork 並調整應用。

● 擴充 Custom GPT 與 Gemini Gem，收錄更多分層適性化的雙語教案範本。

🙏 致謝與回饋交流

由衷感謝我的團隊夥伴們——連續五天全程保持角色設定、編排洗腦舞步賦予主題曲鮮活生命，並且毫無保留地信任一位初任總召「把營隊當成 TRPG 來跑」的瘋狂構想。看著滿室的孩子唱著跳著我們一同做出來的歌曲，那是一份我永遠不會忘記的感動。😭
